subject: internet-packets
title: The Internet's Design Bets
summary: Packet switching, open architecture, and the TCP/IP split as strategic choices.

cards.title: A design that outlived its makers' plans
cards.text: The internet's core protocols were designed in the 1970s for a defense research network. By 1992, the Internet had a million hosts. Which design bets made that scaling possible?

cards.title: Bet 1: share the pipe
cards.text: Circuit switching reserves capacity for a whole session. Packet switching splits data into independently routed packets that share links. Kleinrock published the first paper on packet-switching theory in 1961 and made the case that packets were feasible in place of circuits. ARPANET's first node went live at UCLA in September 1969; four hosts were connected by year-end.

cards.title: Bet 2: don't standardize the networks
cards.text: Kahn's 1972 "open architecture" let independent networks (ARPANET, packet radio, packet satellite) keep their own designs. A common internetworking protocol carried traffic across them. Kahn brought in Vint Cerf in spring 1973 to design what became TCP/IP.
cards.example: Strategy lens: standardize the interface, not the participants. That lowers the cost of joining.

cards.title: Bet 3: a thin waist
cards.text: The original TCP bundled forwarding with reliability. Packet voice experiments in the 1970s showed some applications should handle loss themselves rather than wait for retransmission. So the stack split: IP for addressing and forwarding, TCP for flow control and recovery. The network is best-effort; reliability sits at the edges.

cards.title: Execution
cards.text: DARPA funded three implementations (Stanford, BBN, UCL); within about a year, three independent versions of TCP could interoperate. On January 1, 1983, ARPANET hosts switched from NCP to TCP/IP. ARPA itself was described as a funder of "high-risk, high-gain" research.
cards.example: Per the protocol's designers, email, more than file transfer or remote login, probably had the era's most significant impact.

cards.question: A best-effort core with smart edges made permissionless innovation easy, and it also pushed security and trust problems to the edges. Was that the right trade? What would you choose today?
nudges: Who bears the cost of reliability and security in this design?
Compare it to a platform business you know: open interface vs. controlled network.

questions.q: What prompted splitting the original TCP into TCP and IP?

options.text: Applications like packet voice preferred to handle losses themselves rather than wait for retransmission.
options.why: Right. A thin IP layer left reliability choices to the endpoints.
Email's impact was big, but the split was motivated by applications like voice.

options.text: Security requirements from the Defense Department
options.why: Not the reason given by the protocol's designers.
No. It was an architectural choice.

questions.q: What was the key idea of "open architecture" networking?

options.text: Independent networks keep their own designs and interconnect via a common protocol.
options.why: Standardize the interface, not the networks.
The point was to avoid that requirement.

options.text: Make all network code open source.

questions.q: How was the TCP/IP specification proven in practice?

options.text: Three independently built implementations were shown to interoperate.
options.why: Stanford, BBN, and UCL. Interoperation is the real test of a spec.
No, interoperation required a shared spec.
